region.summary: One-on-one notes with Devon Park covering the ACH pipeline migration and Sidekiq code decommission, the DriveWealth fractional-share reconciliation fix, ADR-032 work, incident follow-ups, and building his staff promotion case.

brief.text:
This region collects the manager's one-on-one notes with Devon Park, a Payments engineer, spanning the ACH pipeline migration, the DriveWealth fractional-share reconciliation problem, ADR-032, incident follow-ups, and the construction of his staff promotion case. Early notes come from a skip-level 1on1 in which Sidekiq ACH stopgap duty was eating roughly a third of Devon's week (slated to move to on-call within two weeks), a shadow-mode diff harness for the ADR-024 outbox worker was required before any cut-over, Payments was understaffed with a senior candidate in final rounds, and Devon said he wanted to grow toward staff with budget, writing time, and mentorship. The new ACH pipeline then completed a 30-day stability hold with zero missed NACHA cutoffs since Aug 18, which approved deletion of the old Sidekiq ACH code; Devon owns the decommission plan. Related incident context: a postmortem (discussed in a 1on1 with Marcus Bell) traced repeated debits to a Sidekiq retry config change plus a round-up sweep job lacking an idempotency key, and Devon's nightly reconciliation alert caught the Sep 26 incident in 47 minutes. Sarah Kim took over the weekly Pillar ops sync, and NACHA cutoff alert tuning remained open.

The reconciliation thread began when Devon found that 0.4% of investing positions drifted from DriveWealth because of split-ratio rounding on corporate-action events; his nightly reconciliation job was catching these breaks. The fix, which consumes DriveWealth corporate-action events and ships with a ready backfill, went into review with an expected landing of Oct 14, and Devon owes a rollout plan before investing go/no-go #2. ADR-032 was drafted to move the round-up sweep onto the outbox pipeline, with Devon leading the build. The manager explicitly sequenced work so that the reconciliation fix goes first and Sidekiq ACH deletion follows no later than Oct 16, because Devon tends to want to fix drift and delete old code at the same time. Later commitment reviews show the fractional-shares write-up and decommission plan done, while the actual code deletion and the written staff case remained open.

Tracked attention items include an open severity-4 risk that dead ACH code can be re-enabled by config (owner Devon), a severity-4 risk that investing GA is blocked by position reconciliation breaks (owner Devon Park), a severity-3 risk that Payments is understaffed and Devon is a retention risk (owner: the manager), a severity-2 risk around Devon's compensation landing after close, and an open todo for the Sidekiq ACH decommission plan. The staff case rests on three pillars: turning his reconciliation design into an org standard, the ADR-032 cross-system build, and mentorship of Sarah Kim. Feedback was that his technical depth is strong but he needs evidence of influence beyond his own code. The case is being written up with Marcus Bell, and the notes record that Devon is now retained through ownership of hard work, though compensation still has to land after close. Typical questions here include when Sidekiq code gets deleted, the status and date of the reconciliation fix, what ADR-032 covers, the basis of Devon's promotion case, and which risks remain open.

items.title: What did we decide after the April 6 ACH outage, and did the follow-ups actually get done?
items.body:
# The April 6 ACH Outage: Decisions and Follow-Up Status

## What happened

On Sunday April 6, Sidekiq workers stalled during the ACH batch and NACHA file generation hung on a rarely used O(n²) serialization path — triggered by a batch of 800+ entries, 35% of them modified-ACH. Sidekiq retries amplified the stall, and the batch missed Pillar Bank's 6 PM PT cutoff. **2,138 auto-deposits totaling $147k were delayed three business days.** No funds were lost. Detection took 25 minutes, root cause within an hour, honest comms out within 5 hours [c2][c8][c26].

Contributing factors: missing tests, no batch-size monitoring, no fallback runbook, and lucky Sunday staffing [c2].

## What you decided

**The architectural decision** — ADR-024, "Move ACH Processing Off Sidekiq." Rails monolith writes to an `ach_outbox` table; a Go outbox relay publishes to the `ach-intents.fifo` SQS queue; a leader-elected `ach-originator` builds and submits files; a separate ingester handles returns. An idempotent state machine moves entries pending → packaged → submitted → settled/returned [c2][c23].

**The policy decisions** — codified customer compensation ($25 credit for any delay caused by your error, rather than deciding live), a Sunday on-call protocol update, and a missed-cutoff protocol agreed with Pillar Bank [c8].

**The four lessons you wrote down:** money movement code paths are tested or removed; known architectural fragility compounds; monitoring is not detection; comms speed beats message polish [c8][c12].

## Did the follow-ups get done? Mostly — eight of nine closed

| Item | Owner | Due | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hotfix the O(n²) serialization | Marcus | Apr 7 | ✅ |
| Batch-size alerts | Marcus | Apr 8 | ✅ |
| Codify $25 compensation policy | Maya | Apr 10 | ✅ |
| ADR for durable ACH pipeline (ADR-024) | Maya | Apr 19 | ✅ |
| Sunday on-call protocol update | Maya | Apr 15 | ✅ |
| Sunday-volume load test passing at 3x | Marcus | Jul 25 | ✅ |
| Customer-comms runbook for delays | Marcus | Jun 2 | ✅ |
| Missed-cutoff protocol with Pillar (Theresa Lowe) | Maya | Jun 4 | ✅ |
| **NACHA-cutoff alerting tuned to page before window closes** | **Marcus** | **2026-10-13** | **❌ Open** |

Source: the published action item list and the Sep 18 status update [c8].

The rebuild itself landed, though late: the first Sunday load test on June 27 failed at 3x, pushing cut-over from end of June to August. Shadow mode ran Aug 4–17, cut-over was Aug 18, and there have been **zero missed cutoffs since** [c8][c9][c19].

## Two things are still open right now — and both are due within days

**1. NACHA-cutoff alert tuning (Marcus, due Oct 13 — two days out).** This is the last original April 6 action item, and it has slipped. Worse, the alert as it stands fires too often on normal Sunday volume. Your own note on it is the sharpest framing in the record: *"An alert people learn to ignore is the April 6 failure mode again"* [c8], echoed in the Oct 2 Pillar ops sync as "Light-day alert noise trains people to ignore the NACHA-cutoff alert, which only exists because of April 6" [c32]. It also appears as an open commitment in your Oct 1 1:1 with Marcus [c22].

**2. Sidekiq ACH code deletion (Devon, due Oct 16).** This is a *downstream* item — not on the original April 6 list, but a direct consequence of the rebuild. The 30-day stability hold ended Sep 17 and the September Pillar MBR approved deletion [c8][c16][c28]. It has now been approved-but-undone for over three weeks. Devon has been on the fractional-share reconciliation fix, which you agreed was the right priority [c29][c31]. The decision from your Oct 7 1:1 was explicit: **recon fix first, Sidekiq deletion immediately after, no later than Oct 16** [c29]. Devon also owes Theresa's team a written deletion notice by Oct 13 [c32].

Your stated reason for urgency is worth repeating back: dead money-moving code that anyone can re-enable with a config change is exactly how Sep 26 happened on a different job [c29][c31]. That's tracked as an open risk ("Dead ACH code re-enableable by config," owner Devon) [c3].

## The honest assessment

The April 6 response was a well-executed postmortem by most standards — the architecture got rebuilt, the pipeline has held clean since August, and eight of nine items closed. But the two items still open are both *detection and hygiene* items, which maps directly onto lesson #3 you wrote in April ("monitoring is not detection") and lesson #1 ("cold paths that exist 'in case' are a liability") [c8][c12]. The structural fix shipped; the two follow-ups that guard against the same failure mode recurring are the ones that slipped.

Note also that Marcus — who owns the one remaining original action item — is flagged in your own 1:1 notes as a burnout risk, "running on fumes and duty," with a week off booked post-GA [c22][c17]. That's likely relevant to why the alert tuning keeps sliding.

One caveat on the Sidekiq deletion item: it's linked to the April 6 thread through the ADR-024 rebuild rather than appearing on the original postmortem checklist, so treating it as an "April 6 follow-up" is a derived connection [c27][c8].
